data.title: One God and the Three Pillars
data.sourcePassage: Sikhism is a monotheistic religion founded in the Punjab region of South Asia in the fifteenth century by Guru Nanak Dev Ji. The foundational belief is expressed in the words Ik Onkar — 'There is one God.' God is known as Waheguru, meaning 'Wonderful Lord', and is understood as the creator of everything, present in all people. Sikhism is built on three foundational pillars that connect belief to daily action. The first is Naam Japna — remembering God by meditating on and reciting God's name throughout the day. The second is Kirat Karni — earning a living through honest, hard work without deception. The third is Vand Chakna — sharing one's wealth, time, and resources with those in need. These three pillars make Sikhism a faith of practical daily action: belief in one God must be expressed through honest living and generous sharing.

data.title: The Gurdwara and the Guru Granth Sahib
data.sourcePassage: The gurdwara — meaning 'Gateway of the Guru' — is the Sikh place of worship and community centre. Outside, the Nishan Sahib (Sikh flag) marks its location. Visitors remove their shoes and cover their heads before entering as signs of respect. In the main prayer hall (darbar sahib), the Guru Granth Sahib — the eternal, living Guru — is placed on a raised throne (takht) under a canopy. Worshippers bow before it when entering, and no one ever sits higher than it. The Guru Granth Sahib is not treated as an ordinary book: it is the living presence of the Guru. A granthi reads from it and kirtan — devotional singing of hymns — fills the hall. The congregation (sangat) sits together on the floor. Attached to every gurdwara is the langar hall, where free vegetarian food is served to all comers, regardless of faith, wealth, or background. Everyone sits on the floor in rows (pangat), expressing the Sikh belief that all people are equal before Waheguru.

data.title: The Khalsa, the Five Ks, and Vaisakhi
data.sourcePassage: In 1699, Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa — the community of initiated Sikhs committed to upholding Sikh values and defending the oppressed. He called for five volunteers willing to give their lives, known as the Panj Pyare (the Five Beloved Ones), and initiated them into the Khalsa at Vaisakhi. Guru Gobind Singh gave initiated Khalsa Sikhs five articles of faith, each beginning with the letter K in Punjabi: Kesh (uncut hair, accepting God's will), Kanga (a wooden comb representing cleanliness), Kara (a steel bracelet reminding the wearer of God's infinity), Kachera (a cotton undergarment representing self-control), and Kirpan (a small ceremonial sword symbolising justice and the defence of the oppressed). Vaisakhi — celebrated each April — is both a harvest festival and the anniversary of the Khalsa's founding, marked by nagar kirtan processions, prayers, and langar. It is the most important Sikh festival. Guru Gobind Singh later declared that after him, the Guru Granth Sahib would be the eternal Guru for all Sikhs.
